analysis.one_liner: Replaces private military contractors with government personnel for security and core war-zone functions.
analysis.headline: The bill died in House committees without a hearing or vote; it never came to the House floor in the 111th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the State Department to stop using armed private security contractors at U.S. embassies in Iraq and Afghanistan within 180 days, and would have begun phasing out private contractors for critical war-zone functions—guards, trainers, interrogators—by January 1, 2011. It would also have opened up Iraq and Afghanistan contracts worth over $5 million for inspection by congressional committees and required reports on contractor costs, casualties, and discipline. It was referred to three House committees and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor time.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who were funding hundreds of thousands of contractor positions in Iraq and Afghanistan, including contracts where auditors said the State Department could not account for what it received for $1.2 billion of police training spending. U.S. military and diplomatic personnel also benefit from ending the use of armed contractors whose conduct, like the 2007 Nisour Square shooting that killed 17 Iraqis, drew findings that it worked 'at cross-purposes' to the mission. Contractor employees themselves gain whistleblower protections and criminal-jurisdiction guarantees the bill would have required.

how_it_helps.text: Required all security at U.S. diplomatic missions in Iraq and Afghanistan to be performed by U.S. government personnel within 180 days of enactment, replacing armed private guards.

Directed planning to replace private contractors for mission-critical functions—protective services, training, interrogation, intelligence—with government and military personnel by January 1, 2011, across all conflict zones where Congress authorized force.

Gave five House and five Senate committees access to every Iraq and Afghanistan contract and task order over $5 million dating back to October 2001, and required reports on contractor headcounts, total costs, deaths and injuries, and disciplinary actions.

Barred renewal of any mission-critical contractor unless the President certified workers passed background checks, faced no pending criminal charges, were subject to U.S. criminal jurisdiction abroad, and the contract included whistleblower protections.

analysis.who_pays: Private military and security contractors, including firms like Blackwater (then Xe Services), DynCorp, and ArmorGroup, would lose the security and mission-critical work the bill phased out. The government would bear the cost of hiring, training, and deploying its own personnel to do that work, and any remaining contractors would face quarterly congressional review of their accounting.

drawbacks.text: Moving security and mission-critical work in-house requires recruiting and training government personnel on a tight timeline while two wars were underway; the bill anticipated this by forcing a Presidential plan and allowing extensions with justification, but an aggressive 2011 deadline risked gaps in security coverage if staffing fell short.

Government personnel are not always cheaper: the bill's own findings cite roughly 218,000 contractor employees versus 195,000 troops in Iraq and Afghanistan, so converting that scale of work to federal employees would carry substantial payroll, benefits, and overhead costs in the near term.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main benefit—restoring public accountability and legal jurisdiction over armed personnel operating in America's name in war zones—addressed documented problems: contractor shootings of civilians, unaccountable billions in billing, and firms whose employees had escaped charges. The real cost is transition risk and near-term expense of building in-house capacity during active wars; the bill tried to manage this with reporting and certification requirements, though the deadlines were ambitious.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on February 23, 2010, with 18 original cosponsors.
The same day it was referred to the House Foreign Affairs, Armed Services, and Intelligence committees.
No further action was recorded; the bill never left committee and received no vote in the House before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private military and security contractors kept their government business, since no phase-out or new oversight requirements took effect. Executive agencies avoided the contract disclosure and quarterly accounting reviews the bill would have imposed on them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private military contractors and contracting agencies

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to phase out private military contractors and documented contractor misconduct in its findings.

against.name: House Foreign Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no recorded action—no hearing or markup—before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no recorded action on the bill.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no recorded action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 30 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill never reached a floor vote, so no record exists of how the full House or either party would have voted.

industries.industry: Private military and security contractors (e.g., Blackwater/Xe, DynCorp, ArmorGroup)
industries.note: The bill would have phased out their core government work—embassy security, protective services, training, interrogation—in conflict zones, and subjected any remaining contracts to quarterly congressional accounting reviews. Its findings cite shootings of civilians, unaccountable billing, and misconduct by these firms that government oversight had failed to correct.

industries.industry: War-zone logistics and support contractors under DOD, State, Interior, and USAID
industries.note: Contracts over $5 million for work in Iraq and Afghanistan would have opened to inspection by congressional committees, and agencies would have had to report headcounts, costs, casualties, and disciplinary actions. Firms performing mission-critical functions could keep contracts only with certifications on background checks and whistleblower protections.
